back: AC has insulated conductors and a bonding strip inside flexible interlocked steel armor. The armor plus the internal aluminum bonding strip form the equipment grounding path. A plastic anti-short bushing sits between the armor and the conductors at each cut end to protect the insulation from the sharp armor edge.

front: What is the difference between Type SE and Type USE service-entrance cable?
back: Type SE has a flame-retardant, moisture-resistant jacket for above-ground use. Type USE is for underground service. Style U is round and style R is flat. For services, the bare neutral under the jacket may serve as the grounded conductor.

front: What is a quarter bend in a conduit run?
back: A quarter bend is one 90 degree bend. The total of all bends between two pull points must not exceed 360 degrees, which equals four quarter bends or any combination of angles adding up to 360 or less. The reason is pulling tension on the conductors.

front: How is burial cover measured under Table 300.5?
back: Cover is the shortest distance from the top surface of the buried cable, conduit or conductor to the top surface of finished grade, concrete or similar cover. It is measured to the top of the cable or conduit, not the bottom of the trench, and a wider or deeper trench does not change the minimum.

front: What is the free conductor rule for a box?
back: At each outlet, junction and switch point at least 6 inches of free conductor must be left, and at least 3 inches of that must extend outside the box opening. This gives enough wire to make the splice or terminate on the device. Conductors cut too short are a common inspection failure.

front: In box fill, how is a pigtail that starts and ends inside the box counted?
back: A conductor that starts and finishes inside the box, such as a pigtail used for a splice, is not counted at all. That is why the length of a pigtail does not matter for box fill. Only conductors that originate outside the box and end or pass through it are counted.

front: What can flexible cords under Article 400 be used for, and what is the key use not permitted?
back: Section 400.10 permits uses such as pendants, portable luminaires, appliances and connecting equipment for frequent interchange. Section 400.12 is the one the exam asks: a flexible cord may not substitute for fixed wiring, run through walls, ceilings, floors or doorways, be attached to building surfaces, or be concealed.

front: What is the minimum distance from the edge of wood framing for a bored hole carrying a cable or raceway, and what if you cannot meet it?
back: The hole must be at least 1-1/4 inches from the nearest edge of the framing member under 300.4. If it must be closer, or the cable runs in a notch, cover it with a steel plate at least 1/16 inch thick. RMC, IMC, EMT and rigid PVC conduit do not need the plate, but cables and flexible raceways do.

front: What are the support intervals for EMT, IMC and RMC, and the rule at terminations?
back: Support them at intervals not exceeding 10 feet and within 3 feet of each outlet box, junction box, device box, cabinet, conduit body or other termination. Longer spans are allowed for straight runs of threaded conduit with wrenchtight couplings, but confirm the table in your 2026 NEC.

front: What are the PVC support spacings for trade sizes 1/2 through 2 inch?
back: From Table 352.30: 1/2 to 1 inch needs support every 3 feet, and 1-1/4 to 2 inch needs support every 5 feet. In addition PVC must be supported within 3 feet of each box, conduit body or termination. Do not apply the 10 foot steel rule to plastic.

front: What are the PVC support spacings for trade sizes 2-1/2 inch and larger?
back: From Table 352.30: 2-1/2 to 3 inch every 6 feet, 3-1/2 to 5 inch every 7 feet, and 6 inch every 8 feet. Still add the support within 3 feet of each box or termination. Supports for PVC are always much closer than for EMT or RMC.

front: What are the support rules for FMC and LFMC?
back: Support FMC and LFMC within 12 inches of each box or termination and at intervals not exceeding 4-1/2 feet. A short exception for flexibility exists at terminations, but confirm it in your 2026 book. Flexible metal conduit is supported much closer than rigid metal conduit.

front: What are the support rules for NM cable under 334.30?
back: Secure NM within 12 inches of every box, cabinet, conduit body or fitting, and at intervals not exceeding 4-1/2 feet. With a single-gang nonmetallic box that has no clamps, secure the cable within 8 inches of the box. In 2026 the staples, straps and hangers must be listed.

front: What is the support interval for MC cable, and how does it differ from NM, AC and SE?
back: MC must be secured at intervals not exceeding 6 feet and within 12 inches of every box or cabinet (330.30). NM, AC and SE are 12 inches from a box and every 4-1/2 feet. The exam likes to swap these two numbers.

front: What are the support spacing rules for ENT, and does it carry ground fault current?
back: ENT is supported within 3 feet of each box and at intervals not exceeding 3 feet. It is flexible corrugated plastic tubing and, like PVC, does not carry ground fault current, so an equipment grounding conductor is required inside it.

front: What are the minimum bending radii for NM cable and for MC cable?
back: NM and AC cable need a bending radius of at least five times the cable diameter (334.24 and 320.24). MC needs ten times the external diameter of the sheath for smooth-sheath types and seven times for interlocked-armor or corrugated types (330.24).

front: What percentage of raceway area may conductors fill for one, two and more than two conductors?
back: Chapter 9 Table 1 allows 53 percent for one conductor, 31 percent for two conductors, and 40 percent for more than two conductors. Every wire counts, including equipment grounding conductors and bonding jumpers, so the green wire counts in both the area and the conductor count.

front: What minimum cover does Table 300.5 give for UF cable, RMC or IMC, PVC listed for direct burial, and GFCI-protected residential circuits?
back: Direct-buried cable such as UF or USE: 24 inches. RMC and IMC: 6 inches. Nonmetallic raceway such as PVC listed for direct burial without concrete: 18 inches. Residential 120 volt, 20 ampere GFCI-protected branch circuits: 12 inches. Read the column that matches the wiring method.

front: What cover is required under a street, and under a one- or two-family dwelling driveway used only for the dwelling?
back: Under streets, highways, roads, alleys, driveways and parking lots the cover is 24 inches for most methods. Under the driveway or outdoor parking area of a one- or two-family dwelling used only for dwelling-related purposes, it is reduced to 18 inches for most methods.

front: How high must underground wiring be protected where it emerges from the ground?
back: It must be protected from physical damage to a height of 8 feet above finished grade, or to the point of entry into the building, using RMC, IMC, Schedule 80 PVC or another approved method (300.5(D)). A bushing or terminal fitting must also protect conductors where they emerge from an underground raceway as direct burial wiring (300.5(H)).

front: What volume does Table 314.16(A) give for a 3 by 2 by 3-1/2 inch device box and for 4 inch square boxes 1-1/2 and 2-1/8 inches deep?
back: A 3 by 2 by 3-1/2 inch device box holds 18 cubic inches, and a 3 by 2 by 2-3/4 inch box holds 14. A 4 inch square box 1-1/2 inches deep holds 21 and one 2-1/8 inches deep holds 30.3. A 4-11/16 inch square box 2-1/8 inches deep holds 42. A marked volume on the box overrides the table.

front: What volume allowance per conductor does Table 314.16(B) give for 14, 12, 10, 8 and 6 AWG?
back: 14 AWG takes 2.00 cubic inches, 12 AWG takes 2.25, 10 AWG takes 2.50, 8 AWG takes 3.00 and 6 AWG takes 5.00 cubic inches. Conductors of 4 AWG and larger are handled under 314.28 for pull boxes instead of box fill.

front: What are the box fill allowances for equipment grounding conductors, clamps, support fittings and devices?
back: All equipment grounding conductors together count as one allowance, based on the largest. Internal clamps count as one allowance, based on the largest conductor. Support fittings count as one allowance for each type. Each device yoke counts as two, based on the largest conductor connected to that device.

front: How are straight pulls and angle pulls sized under 314.28 for conductors 4 AWG and larger?
back: A straight pull needs a box length of at least eight times the trade size of the largest raceway. An angle or U pull needs the entry-to-opposite-wall distance of at least six times the largest raceway, plus the sum of the other raceways on the same wall and row.

front: What working space does 110.26 require in front of a panelboard rated 150 volts to ground or less?
back: The clear depth is 3 feet, the width at least 30 inches or the width of the equipment whichever is greater, and the headroom at least 6-1/2 feet. The space above, up to 6 feet or the ceiling, is also reserved so piping and ducts do not cross it.

front: What is the maximum height of the top operating handle of a breaker or switch, and where may a dwelling OCPD not be located?
back: The highest operating handle in its highest position must not be more than 6 feet 7 inches above the floor or working platform (240.24(A)). In a dwelling unit an overcurrent device may not be in a bathroom, a clothes closet, where ignitable material is stored, or over stairway steps.

front: What fill limits apply to wiring space in a switch or OCPD enclosure under 312.8?
back: Conductors at any cross section must not fill more than 40 percent of the cross-sectional area of the space they occupy. Splices, taps and feed-through conductors must not fill more than 75 percent at that cross section. Confirm the exact wording in your book.

front: A 4 inch square box (30.3 cubic inches) holds six 14 AWG conductors, one 14 AWG ground, internal clamps and two switches on 14 AWG. Does it pass?
back: Count allowances at 2.00 cubic inches each for 14 AWG: 6 conductors, 1 ground, 1 clamp set and 2 switches at two each is 4, for 12 allowances. 12 times 2.00 equals 24.00 cubic inches. That is under 30.3, so it passes with 6.30 cubic inches to spare.

front: A 14 cubic inch box holds four 14 AWG conductors from outside, one ground, no clamps and one receptacle on 14 AWG. Does it pass?
back: Allowances: 4 conductors, 1 ground, and 2 for the receptacle, which is 7 allowances. Each is 2.00 cubic inches from Table 314.16(B) for 14 AWG, so 7 times 2.00 equals 14.00 cubic inches. The fill equals the volume, which is permitted, so it passes with nothing to spare.

front: A box has five 12 AWG conductors from outside, a 12 AWG pigtail starting and ending inside, one ground and no clamps or devices. What is the fill?
back: The pigtail is not counted. Count 5 conductors plus 1 allowance for the grounds, which is 6 allowances at 2.25 cubic inches for 12 AWG. 6 times 2.25 equals 13.50 cubic inches. Adding the pigtail would give the wrong answer, 15.75.

front: Six 12 AWG THHN conductors and one 12 AWG THHN equipment grounding conductor go into EMT. Using 0.0133 square inch each and the 40 percent column, what is the smallest trade size?
back: Seven conductors count, the ground included: 7 times 0.0133 equals 0.0931 square inch. At 40 percent, 1/2 inch EMT offers 0.122 square inch, which is larger than 0.0931. So 1/2 inch EMT is enough. More than two conductors means the 40 percent rule.

front: Eight 10 AWG THHN conductors (0.0211 square inch each) are pulled into EMT. Using the 40 percent column, what is the smallest trade size?
back: Total area is 8 times 0.0211, which equals 0.1688 square inch. In Table 4 at 40 percent for EMT, 1/2 inch offers 0.122, which is too small. 3/4 inch offers 0.213, which is enough. The answer is 3/4 inch EMT.

front: Two 1/0 THHN conductors (0.1855 square inch each) go in EMT. At 31 percent, 1 inch EMT is 0.346 at 40 percent and 1-1/4 inch is 0.598 at 40 percent. What size is needed?
back: Total area is 2 times 0.1855, which equals 0.371 square inch. Two conductors allow 31 percent. Scale each 40 percent area by 0.31 over 0.40: 1 inch gives 0.268 and 1-1/4 inch gives 0.463. 0.268 is too small, 0.463 is enough, so use 1-1/4 inch EMT.

front: How many 12 AWG THHN conductors (0.0133 square inch each) fit in 1 inch EMT, which has 0.346 square inch at 40 percent?
back: Divide the allowed area by one conductor's area: 0.346 divided by 0.0133 equals 26.02. Always round down because a fraction of a wire does not fit, so the answer is 26 conductors. This shortcut works only when all conductors are the same size and insulation.

front: An 18 inch EMT nipple carries four 6 AWG THHN conductors (0.0507 square inch each). 3/4 inch EMT is 0.213 square inch at 40 percent. Does 3/4 inch work?
back: The nipple is under 24 inches, so 60 percent applies. The 60 percent area of 3/4 inch is 0.213 divided by 0.40 times 0.60, which equals 0.3195 square inch. The total is 4 times 0.0507, which equals 0.2028. That is less than 0.3195, so 3/4 inch works.

front: A straight pull box takes conductors of 4 AWG and larger through 2-1/2 inch conduits on opposite ends. What is the minimum box length?
back: A straight pull must be at least eight times the trade size of the largest raceway under 314.28. Eight times 2-1/2 inches equals 20 inches. If you used the angle-pull multiple of six you would get 15 inches, which is wrong for a straight pull.

front: An angle pull has a 3 inch, a 2 inch and a 1-1/2 inch conduit on the same wall. What minimum distance is needed to the opposite wall?
back: Use six times the largest raceway plus the sum of the others on that wall. Six times 3 inches equals 18 inches. Add 2 inches plus 1-1/2 inches, which is 3.5 inches. The total is 21.5 inches. The box must be at least 21.5 inches in that dimension.

front: A run has three 90 degree bends, one 45 degree bend and two 30 degree bends between pull points. Is it legal?
back: Add the angles: 3 times 90 equals 270, plus 45 equals 315, plus 60 equals 375 degrees. The limit is 360 degrees between pull points, so 375 exceeds it. A pull box or conduit body is required to restart the count, and the limit also holds across different raceway types in 2026.

front: PVC is installed outdoors in a 150 foot run with a 60 degree F temperature swing. Using 0.0406 inch per degree F per 100 feet, how much will it grow?
back: Growth per 100 feet is 0.0406 times 60, which equals 2.436 inches. For 150 feet multiply by 1.5: 3.654, about 3.65 inches. That is well over the 1/4 inch trigger of 352.44, so expansion fittings are required. Check Table 352.44 in your book.

front: How many staples are needed for a 15 foot run of NM cable between two boxes, first one 1 foot from a box and last one 1 foot from the other?
back: The span between the first staple at 1 foot and the last at 14 feet is 13 feet. Maximum spacing is 4-1/2 feet, and 13 divided by 4.5 is 2.9, so three gaps are needed. Three gaps means four staples, counting both ends. Support 12 inches from each box.

front: What is the allowable ampacity of 12 AWG NM cable when 12 current-carrying conductors are bundled, with 90 degree C conductors at 30 amperes and a 50 percent factor for 10 to 20 conductors?
back: Adjusted ampacity is 30 times 0.50, which equals 15 amperes. NM ampacity may never exceed the 60 degree C column, which is 20 amperes for 12 AWG. The lower value controls, so 15 amperes, and a 20 ampere breaker is no longer allowed for that circuit.

front: How many supports are needed for a 35 foot run of EMT between two boxes?
back: EMT needs support within 3 feet of each box and at intervals not exceeding 10 feet. Supports at 3, 13, 23 and 33 feet work: the first is within 3 feet of the first box, each gap is 10 feet, and the last is 2 feet from the second box. The answer is four supports.

front: A question gives two 4 AWG conductors in EMT. Which fill percentage applies, and what is the trap?
back: Two conductors allow 31 percent of the raceway area from Chapter 9 Table 1. The trap is using 40 percent, which applies only to more than two conductors, or 53 percent, which applies to one. Count the green equipment grounding conductor too, since it changes the number of conductors.

front: In box fill, a candidate counts each ground wire separately. What does the rule actually say?
back: All equipment grounding conductors in the box together count as one allowance, based on the largest one. An isolated equipment grounding conductor gets its own separate allowance. Counting each ground wire is a common wrong answer that makes a passing box look too small.

front: When counting a device in box fill, which conductor size sets the allowance, and what is the trap?
back: A device counts as two allowances based on the largest conductor connected to that device, not the largest conductor in the box. Clamp and grounding allowances use the largest conductor in the whole box. A switch landed only on 14 AWG counts two times 2.00 even if 12 AWG is present.

front: What is the trap in mixing up Table 314.16(A) and Table 314.16(B)?
back: Table 314.16(A) gives box volumes in cubic inches, and Table 314.16(B) gives the volume allowance per conductor. Many wrong answers are the right number from the wrong table. Also never apply the box-fill method to pull boxes, which are sized under 314.28 for conductors of 4 AWG and larger.

front: Does PVC conduit need a separate equipment grounding conductor, and does EMT?
back: PVC is not a conductor, so an equipment grounding conductor must run inside it (352.60), sized from Table 250.122. EMT can serve as the equipment grounding conductor when installed with proper fittings. LFNC and ENT, like PVC, always need a separate grounding conductor.

front: What ampacity column must be used for NM cable even if the conductor insulation is rated 90 degrees C?
back: Use the 60 degree C column of Table 310.16 (334.80). The 90 degree C insulation rating, such as THHN, may be used only for adjustment and correction calculations. For example, 12 AWG NM is 20 amperes from the 60 degree C column.

front: A run between two boxes has a pull box in the middle. Does the 360 degree bend limit count the whole run?
back: No. The limit applies between pull points, so a pull box or a conduit body used as a pull point restarts the count. A simple coupling does not restart it. However, changing raceway type does not reset the count, because the 2026 section 300.24 says the limit applies across types.

front: May NM cable be buried directly in the ground, and in what buildings is NM not permitted?
back: NM is never buried directly. UF is the cable that goes underground. NM is permitted in one- and two-family dwellings, multifamily dwellings and other structures of Type III, IV or V construction, but not in Type I and Type II construction (334.10 and 334.12).

front: An electrician mounts a ceiling fan on an ordinary ceiling outlet box. What is wrong?
back: A ceiling-suspended fan needs a box listed for the support of a fan, and a fan over 35 pounds needs a box marked with its maximum weight (314.27(C)). An ordinary ceiling box is not enough. A luminaire over 50 pounds must also be supported independently of the box unless the box is listed for it.

front: A flexible cord is run through a wall to feed a fixed appliance. Is that permitted?
back: No. Under 400.12 a flexible cord may not substitute for the fixed wiring of a structure, may not run through holes in walls, ceilings or floors, and may not be concealed behind them. A cord is for portable or movable equipment, not for fixed wiring.

front: Can ampacity adjustment be skipped just because the conductors physically fit in the raceway?
back: No. Raceway fill and ampacity adjustment are two separate questions. A raceway may physically hold 20 wires, but with 21 to 30 current-carrying conductors each wire's ampacity is reduced to 45 percent under 310.15(C)(1), and 10 to 20 conductors give 50 percent. Always ask whether it fits and whether the ampacity still works.

front: How do you find the right section for a wiring method fast in an open-book exam, using EMT as an example?
back: Remember the article family: EMT is Article 358. Then use the fixed section pattern, so the number of bends is 358.26 and the supports are 358.30. Tab Article 300, Article 314 with Table 314.16(A), the Chapter 9 tables, and Table 300.5 in advance.

front: What did 2026 add in 300.4(C) about damaged wiring?
back: Conductors and wiring methods no longer suitable for use because of overheating, fire damage, corrosive influences or water must be replaced. Informational notes cite NEMA GD 1-2019 for water-damaged equipment and GD 2-2021 for fire- and heat-damaged equipment. A flooded or fire-affected installation cannot just be dried out and reused.

front: What is new section 300.24 in the 2026 NEC?
back: It clarifies that the 360 degree bend limit applies to the run as a whole even when the run changes from one raceway type to another. If a run goes EMT, then flexible metal conduit, then PVC, the bends in all three are added together. Confirm the section number in your printed book.

front: What did the 2026 NEC change for locknuts on IMC and RMC, and for dissimilar metals?
back: Section 342.29 for IMC and 344.29 for RMC require paired locknuts, one inside and one outside the enclosure. Section 342.14 requires bimetallic couplings, identified to prevent galvanic corrosion, where two different metals are joined. Confirm the section numbers in your printed 2026 book.

front: What new support-hardware listing rules did 2026 add for cable and cable ties?
back: Articles 320, 330, 332, 334, 336 and 340 now require listing of cable ties, staples, straps and hangers used with AC, MC, MI, NM, NMC, TC and UF cable, with UL 2239 as the referenced standard. Section 300.13(E) says cable ties for securement must be listed and identified for that purpose.

front: What 2026 access-space rule applies above a cable tray?
back: Section 392.18(F) requires a minimum 12 inch access space above a cable tray. Four exceptions allow the authority having jurisdiction to grant special permission for information technology installations and for industrial locations with qualified personnel. Confirm the details in your printed 2026 book.

front: What does 408.6 require for panelboards in the 2026 NEC?
back: Switchboards and panelboards must have a short-circuit current rating at least equal to the available fault current at their line side. In other than one- and two-family dwellings, the available fault current and the calculation date must be field marked at the point of supply, and the calculation documented.

front: What did 2026 change for roof decking protection and for reconditioned cabinets?
back: Section 300.6(E) now covers all roof deck types, not only metal-corrugated, and applies to wiring methods and equipment, with an exception for wiring encased in at least 2 inches of concrete in concealed locations. Section 312.3 prohibits reconditioned cabinets, cutout boxes and meter socket enclosures.

front: Which new 2026 articles might you land on while searching the index, and are they your branch-circuit answer?
back: Article 305 covers general requirements over 1,000 volts ac or 1,500 volts dc, and Article 315 covers medium-voltage cable from 2,001 to 35,000 volts ac. Article 395 content moved into Article 267. They are not your usual 600 volt or less answer, so keep looking.

front: Which Chapter 9 tables do you use for conduit fill, and in what order?
back: First find each conductor's area in Table 5 and add them. Then pick the fill percentage from Table 1: 53, 31 or 40 percent. Then use Table 4 to find the smallest trade size of that raceway type whose area at that percentage is at least your total. Annex C is a shortcut only for same-size conductors.

front: Which article do you open first for a question about a household range, and what second source gives its demand?
back: Article 422 covers appliances such as ranges. The demand for household cooking equipment comes from the range demand table (Table 220.55 in older editions, now in Article 120 in the 2026 NEC). Name the equipment first, then find its article, then read the rule.

front: Why can an air conditioner circuit have a breaker larger than the 240.4 conductor rule would suggest?
back: Specific rules override general ones. Article 440 lets the compressor branch circuit device be up to 175 percent of the rated load current, and 240.4(G) is the cross reference that sends you there. The general rule of protecting a conductor at its ampacity does not control.

front: What does the exam instruction say about exceptions, optional methods and conductor material in equipment questions?
back: Ignore exceptions and optional calculation methods unless the question tells you to use them, and treat all conductors as copper unless told otherwise. Nameplate numbers answer half the problem, and your job is to add the Code multiplier that goes with them.

front: What voltage decides the column in Table 110.26(A)(1): line to line or voltage to ground?
back: Voltage to ground decides it. A 480Y/277 system has 277 volts to ground, so it uses the 151 to 600 volt row. A 208Y/120 or 120/240 volt panel has 120 volts to ground, so it uses the 0 to 150 volt row and needs only 3 feet.

front: What working space depths does Table 110.26(A)(1) give for 151 to 600 volts to ground?
back: Condition 1 is 3 feet, Condition 2 is 3 and one half feet, and Condition 3 is 4 feet. For 0 to 150 volts to ground the depth is 3 feet in every condition. Pick the condition from what sits across from the live parts.

front: Define Conditions 1, 2 and 3 for working space depth.
back: Condition 1: live parts on one side only, or on both sides guarded by insulating material. Condition 2: live parts on one side and grounded parts on the other. Condition 3: exposed live parts on both sides with the worker between them.

front: A 480Y/277 volt panel faces a poured concrete wall. What is the minimum working space depth?
back: 3 feet 6 inches. The voltage to ground is about 277, so the 151 to 600 row applies. Concrete counts as a grounded part, so this is Condition 2, which is 3 and one half feet. A 3 foot clearance would be a violation.

front: The same panel faces the same concrete wall but is a 208Y/120 volt system. What depth is required?
back: 3 feet. The voltage to ground is 120, so the 0 to 150 volt row applies and the depth is 3 feet in every condition. The trap is reading 208 volts and wrongly using the 3 and one half foot value.

front: Two 480Y/277 volt panelboards with exposed live parts face each other across an aisle. What depth does each need?
back: 4 feet each. Live parts on both sides of the worker is Condition 3 in the 151 to 600 volt row. The working spaces may overlap each other, but each panel still needs its own 4 feet plus the required width and height.

front: How wide must the working space be in front of a 20 inch wide panel, and in front of a 42 inch switchboard?
back: 30 inches for the 20 inch panel and 42 inches for the switchboard. Width is the width of the equipment or 30 inches, whichever is greater. The space need not be centered on the equipment and may overlap the working space of other equipment.

front: What is the minimum height of the working space, and how is it different from the 6 feet 7 inch handle limit?
back: Working space height is the equipment height or 6 and one half feet, whichever is greater, a headroom limit. The 6 feet 7 inch figure is a reach limit: the center of the operating handle grip, in its highest position, cannot be above 6 feet 7 inches.

front: When does 110.26(C)(2) require entrances at each end of the working space?
back: When the equipment is rated 1,200 amperes or more and is over 6 feet wide, unless an exception is met. In the 2026 NEC this large equipment rule covers feeder disconnecting means too, not only service disconnecting means.

front: What is the dedicated space above a panelboard, and what may not be in it?
back: The space equal to the width and depth of the equipment, from the floor up to 6 feet above the equipment or to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower. Piping, ducts and foreign equipment cannot be in it, even if they never touch the panel.

front: What new requirement does the 2026 NEC add about equipment doors in 110.26?
back: Equipment doors, when opened to 90 degrees, must not block the required egress path, which is 24 inches wide and 6 and one half feet high. Measure with the doors at 90 degrees even if they can open farther.

front: How large an overcurrent device may feed a panelboard under 408.36, and can a 200 ampere panelboard be fed by a 225 ampere breaker?
back: No. The supply side overcurrent device cannot be rated more than the panelboard rating. A 200 ampere panelboard cannot be fed from a 225 ampere breaker. The panel may be larger than its feeder device, but never smaller.

front: In a subpanel, how are the neutral and equipment grounding conductor handled?
back: They stay separate. The neutral bar is bonded to the enclosure only at the service or at the first disconnect of a separately derived system. That is why you remove the bonding screw or strap in a subpanel. Panelboards need an equipment grounding terminal bar.

front: How is the high leg identified on a 4 wire delta system, and where does it land in the panel?
back: The conductor with the higher voltage to ground is marked with an orange outer finish or other effective means (110.15). It lands on the B phase position, the center. It measures about 208 volts to ground and cannot supply 120 volt single pole loads.

front: What does 408.6 require in the 2026 NEC for switchboards and panelboards?
back: The short-circuit current rating must be not less than the available fault current at the supply side. Other than one and two family dwellings, field mark the available fault current, the calculation date and the SCCR, document the calculation, and update it after modifications.

front: A 208Y/120 volt, 3 phase panelboard serves 40 kVA continuous and 12 kVA noncontinuous load. What are the calculated kVA and amperes?
back: Calculated load is 40 times 1.25 plus 12, which is 62 kVA. Amperes equal 62,000 divided by (1.732 times 208), or 62,000 divided by 360.3, which is 172.1 amperes. The next standard overcurrent device is 175 amperes.

front: In the 62 kVA, 172.1 ampere panelboard problem, what are the device and panelboard ratings, and which three mistakes does the exam set?
back: The device is 175 amperes (240.6(A) size) and the panelboard is 200 amperes. The traps are dropping the 125 percent continuous factor (about 144 amperes), using 120 volts instead of 208 and 1.732, or using 1.732 on a single phase system.

front: When may you round up to the next standard OCPD size under 240.4(B)?
back: Only when the conductor ampacity does not match a standard rating, the rating does not exceed 800 amperes, and the circuit is not a multi-outlet branch circuit supplying receptacles for cord and plug connected portable loads.

front: What are the small conductor OCPD limits in 240.4(D) for copper 14, 12 and 10 AWG?
back: 14 AWG copper is limited to 15 amperes, 12 AWG to 20 amperes and 10 AWG to 30 amperes, even though Table 310.16 may show more. A 10 AWG wire shows 35 amperes at 75 degrees C but still stops at a 30 ampere OCPD.

front: What is the branch circuit OCPD rule for continuous loads in 210.20(A), and what counts as continuous?
back: The OCPD must be at least the noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of the continuous load. A continuous load is one where the maximum current is expected to continue for 3 hours or more. Section 215.3 applies the same rule to feeders.

front: Under 110.14(C), which Table 310.16 column applies for circuits of 100 amperes or less, and for those above 100 amperes?
back: For 100 amperes or less, or conductors 14 AWG through 1 AWG, use the 60 degree C column unless the equipment is listed and identified for 75 degrees C. Above 100 amperes, use the 75 degree C column.

front: What does a slash voltage rating such as 120/240 on a breaker mean?
back: The breaker is suitable only on a solidly grounded system where no conductor is more than the lower number to ground. A 277/480 slash rated breaker can serve single pole loads on 480Y/277. Corner grounded or ungrounded systems need a straight rated breaker.

front: What is the difference between a device's interrupting rating and an assembly's short-circuit current rating?
back: The interrupting rating belongs to the device, the fault current it can open without failing (110.9). The short-circuit current rating belongs to the assembly, such as a panelboard. A breaker with the right ampere rating can still fail if its interrupting rating is too low.

front: A 75 kVA, 208Y/120 volt, 3 phase transformer has 2.5 percent impedance with an infinite primary source. What is the secondary fault current?
back: Full load current is 75,000 divided by (1.732 times 208), or 75,000 divided by 360.3, which is 208.2 amperes. Divide by 0.025 to get about 8,328 amperes. A 10,000 ampere interrupting rating is acceptable.

front: For the same 75 kVA, 208Y/120 volt transformer, what is the fault current if impedance is 1.5 percent, and what breaker rating is needed?
back: 208.2 amperes divided by 0.015 equals about 13,880 amperes. A 10,000 ampere breaker would fail 110.9, so you need at least 14,000 amperes interrupting. Lower transformer impedance means higher available fault current.

front: Which fuse classes of 600 volts or less does the chapter name, and which are current limiting?
back: Classes J, L, RK1, RK5, CC and T. All are current limiting. Classes J, CC and T have very high interrupting ratings, and the dimensions of the fuse and holder prevent replacing a smaller fuse with a larger one. Dual element time delay fuses suit motor circuits.

front: What does the 2026 NEC say about the scope of Article 406 and where plain wall switch rules may be found?
back: Article 406 now covers wiring devices in general: receptacles, cord connectors, attachment plugs, snap switches, dimmers and electronic control switches. Small switch-type devices moved from Article 404 into 406, so check your own table of contents.

front: According to Table 210.21(B)(3), what receptacle ratings are allowed on 20, 30 and 40 ampere circuits?
back: A 20 ampere circuit takes 15 or 20 ampere receptacles. A 30 ampere circuit takes 30 ampere receptacles. A 40 ampere circuit takes 40 or 50 ampere receptacles. A single receptacle on an individual branch circuit must be rated not less than the circuit.

front: What is the maximum cord and plug connected load on a circuit with two or more receptacles under Table 210.21(B)(2)?
back: 15 or 20 ampere circuit with 15 ampere receptacles: 12 amperes. 20 ampere circuit with 20 ampere receptacles: 16 amperes. 30 ampere circuit with 30 ampere receptacles: 24 amperes. These values are 80 percent of the circuit rating.

front: Three portable heaters at 6 amperes each are on one 20 ampere circuit with 15 ampere receptacles. Is it acceptable?
back: No. The total is 18 amperes, but the limit for 15 ampere receptacles on a 20 ampere circuit is 12 amperes. The circuit is overloaded under the receptacle rule even though 18 is below 20.

front: When a receptacle is replaced in a location that now requires GFCI, tamper resistant or AFCI protection, what must the new one meet?
back: The new receptacle must meet the requirement for the location: GFCI protected where GFCI is required, tamper resistant where required in a dwelling, and AFCI protected where AFCI is required. Replacement does not grandfather the old type.

front: A receptacle is replaced and there is no equipment grounding conductor at the outlet. What does 406.4(D)(2) allow?
back: You may replace it with another nongrounding receptacle, or with a GFCI type marked No Equipment Ground, or connect a grounding receptacle to a GFCI protected circuit with the proper marking. A GFCI receptacle is the usual exam answer.

front: Which occupancies require tamper resistant receptacles, and does mounting height ever exempt them?
back: Dwelling units, guest rooms and suites of hotels and motels, child care facilities, preschools, elementary education facilities, clinic and medical office waiting areas and others listed in 406.12. Receptacles more than 5 and one half feet above the floor are exempt, so check the exceptions.

front: What is the difference between damp and wet location receptacle covers under 406.9?
back: In a damp location the enclosure must be weatherproof when the plug is not inserted. In a wet location it must be weatherproof whether or not the plug is inserted, an in-use cover. A bubble cover is not enough for a pressure washer in a wet location.

front: What is the NEMA configuration for a 15 ampere 125 volt, a 20 ampere 125 volt, a 4 wire range and a 4 wire dryer receptacle?
back: 5-15, 5-20, 14-50 for the range and 14-30 for the dryer. The first number is the configuration family and the second is the ampere rating. A T-slot receptacle is a 20 ampere receptacle that also accepts a 15 ampere plug.

front: How much motor load may a general-use snap switch control, and what horsepower limit applies?
back: A motor load cannot exceed 80 percent of the switch ampere rating, and the motor must be 2 horsepower or less. A 20 ampere general-use AC snap switch can therefore control a motor with a full load current up to 16 amperes.

front: What is the mounting height limit for a snap switch handle?
back: The center of the grip of the operating handle, in its highest position, cannot be more than 6 feet 7 inches above the floor or working platform. A row of gym switches at 7 feet is a violation unless an exception applies.

front: What must be present at a switch outlet that controls lighting in new work, and why does it matter for switch loops?
back: A grounded circuit conductor (neutral) must be present in the box for electronic lighting controls in many cases, with exceptions. Older switch loops with only a hot and a switched hot are no longer the new work default.

front: Where must luminaires in bathtub and shower zones be marked for damp or wet locations?
back: Within the outside dimensions of the tub or shower and extending 8 feet vertically from the top of the tub rim or shower threshold, the luminaire must be marked for damp locations, or for wet locations where subject to shower spray (410.10(D)).

front: What closet clearances does the chapter give for surface mounted and recessed luminaires?
back: Surface mounted incandescent or LED with an enclosed source: 12 inches. Surface mounted fluorescent: 6 inches. Recessed incandescent or LED with an enclosed source: 6 inches. Recessed fluorescent: 6 inches. The trap is flipping 12 and 6, so confirm against your 2026 book.

front: How much weight may a luminaire outlet box support, and when must a luminaire have independent support?
back: An outlet box can support up to 50 pounds unless it is listed and marked for more (314.27(A)(2)). A luminaire over 50 pounds must be supported independently of the box. A 60 pound chandelier on an old work plastic box fails on both counts.

front: What clearances apply to a recessed luminaire that is not Type IC?
back: At least one half inch of space from combustible material except at points of support, and thermal insulation at least 3 inches away from the enclosure, wiring compartment or ballast (410.116). Type IC housings may touch insulation, so choose IC when an attic will be insulated later.

front: A 277 volt, 20 ampere store lighting circuit is continuous. How many 300 volt ampere LED troffers fit?
back: Continuous load is limited to 80 percent of 20, which is 16 amperes. 16 times 277 equals 4,432 volt amperes. 4,432 divided by 300 equals 14.8, so round down to 14 troffers. A fifteenth would exceed the limit.

front: How many 85 volt ampere luminaires fit on a 120 volt, 20 ampere continuous branch circuit?
back: 80 percent of 20 amperes is 16 amperes. 16 times 120 equals 1,920 volt amperes. 1,920 divided by 85 equals 22.6, so round down to 22 luminaires, because part of a luminaire is not a luminaire.

front: Why does a hermetic motor-compressor use its nameplate instead of the Article 430 motor tables?
back: A hermetic refrigerant motor-compressor is sealed in the same housing as its motor and draws current differently from an open motor. Article 440 says use the nameplate rated load current (RLC) or branch circuit selection current (BCSC), whichever is greater, for sizing.

front: What do MCA and MOCP on an air conditioner nameplate stand for, and how do you use them?
back: Minimum circuit ampacity and maximum overcurrent protective device, the Code's minimum supply circuit conductor ampacity and maximum branch circuit protective device ratings (440.4(B)). On the exam, use the printed values as given rather than recomputing.

front: How is the conductor sized for a single motor-compressor under 440.32?
back: At least 125 percent of the rated load current or branch circuit selection current, whichever is greater. For equipment with other motors under 440.33, use 125 percent of the largest compressor current plus the full load currents of the other motors and loads.

front: What is the maximum OCPD for a single motor-compressor under 440.22(A), and how far may it be raised for starting?
back: Up to 175 percent of the rated load current or BCSC, whichever is greater, using the next smaller standard size if it falls between sizes. If that cannot start the compressor, it may be increased but not above 225 percent.

front: What is the minimum disconnect rating for air conditioning equipment, and where must it be located?
back: At least 115 percent of the nameplate rated load current or BCSC (the sum of currents for multiple loads, times 1.15). Under 440.14 it must be within sight of and readily accessible from the equipment, and not on panels removed for servicing.

front: A condensing unit has a compressor RLC of 20.1 amperes and a 1.5 ampere fan at 240 volts. What are the MCA and wire size?
back: MCA equals 20.1 times 1.25 plus 1.5, which is 26.6 amperes. Use the 60 degree C column: 12 AWG gives 25 amperes, too low, and 10 AWG gives 30 amperes. The answer is 10 AWG copper.

front: For the same condensing unit (20.1 ampere compressor, 1.5 ampere fan), what is the maximum overcurrent device?
back: 20.1 times 1.75 equals 35.175, plus 1.5 equals 36.675 amperes. Standard sizes are 35 and 40. The maximum may not be exceeded, so drop to 35 amperes. This is why a 10 AWG conductor can have a 35 ampere breaker.

front: A walk-in cooler compressor has a 16.0 ampere RLC at 240 volts, single phase, with no BCSC. Find the conductor ampacity and the initial breaker size.
back: Conductor: 16.0 times 1.25 equals 20.0 amperes, so 12 AWG copper at 60 degrees C (25 amperes) works. Breaker: 16.0 times 1.75 equals 28.0, between 25 and 30, so take 25 amperes. For hard starting, up to 225 percent (36.0) allows 35 amperes.

front: A rooftop unit has a 24 ampere compressor, 2.4 ampere condenser fan and 4.8 ampere blower. What is the minimum circuit ampacity and the conductor?
back: 24 times 1.25 equals 30, plus 2.4 plus 4.8 equals 37.2 amperes. Table 310.16 at 60 degrees C calls for 8 AWG copper, which carries 40 amperes. Only the largest compressor gets the 125 percent factor.

front: What are the room air conditioner limits on a branch circuit under Part VII of Article 440?
back: If the unit is the only load, its marked rated load current cannot exceed 80 percent of the circuit rating (12 amperes on 15, 16 on 20). If the circuit also serves lighting or other receptacles, the air conditioner is limited to 50 percent.

front: Where must a service receptacle for rooftop HVAC equipment be, and what circuit can it not be on?
back: On the same level and within 25 feet of heating, air conditioning and refrigeration equipment on rooftops, in attics and in crawl spaces (210.63). It cannot be connected on the load side of the equipment disconnect, so it stays live when the disconnect opens.

front: What branch circuit rule applies to fixed electric space heating under 424.3(B)?
back: Branch circuit conductor ampacity and overcurrent device rating must be not less than 125 percent of the total load of the heaters and motors. Treat all fixed electric space heating as continuous. A 3,000 watt, 240 volt heater draws 12.5 amperes, so 15.6 amperes after the 125 percent factor.

front: A 3,000 watt, 240 volt baseboard heater is the only load on the circuit. What breaker and wire?
back: Current is 3,000 divided by 240, which is 12.5 amperes. Times 1.25 equals 15.625 amperes, so a 15 ampere breaker is too small. Use a 20 ampere, 2 pole breaker with 12 AWG copper.

front: When must heating elements be subdivided under 424.22, and what are the limits?
back: Elements of equipment over 48 amperes must be subdivided into loads of no more than 48 amperes each, and each subdivided load is protected by an overcurrent device of no more than 60 amperes. The supply conductors are then sized on the total load.

front: A 20 kilowatt electric furnace at 240 volts, single phase: find current, supply conductor and supply OCPD.
back: Current is 20,000 divided by 240, which is 83.33 amperes. Times 1.25 equals 104.2 amperes. Over 100 amperes uses the 75 degree C column: 3 AWG gives 100 (too low), 2 AWG gives 115, so 2 AWG copper. The next standard OCPD is 110 amperes.

front: What disconnect requirement applies to permanently connected appliances under 422.31, and what serves a cord and plug appliance?
back: Permanently connected appliances over 300 volt amperes or one eighth horsepower need a disconnect within sight, or one that can be locked open. For cord and plug appliances, the attachment plug and receptacle are the disconnect (422.33) if the plug is accessible.

front: A 4,500 watt, 240 volt, 50 gallon storage water heater: find the breaker and wire.
back: A fixed storage water heater of 120 gallons or less is continuous. 4,500 divided by 240 equals 18.75 amperes, times 1.25 equals 23.44 amperes. Twelve AWG is limited to 20 amperes, so use 10 AWG copper with a minimum 25 ampere breaker.

front: What minimum branch circuit does a household range of 8.75 kVA or more need, and what receptacle and wiring do new circuits use?
back: A branch circuit of at least 40 amperes (210.19(A)(3)). New range circuits are 4 wire with a 14-50 receptacle, and dryer circuits use a 14-30. The 3 wire arrangement using the neutral as the frame ground is for existing installations only (250.140).

front: What is the Column C demand for one range not over 12 kW, and how do you adjust a larger one?
back: 8 kilowatts for one range, 11 for two, 14 for three, 17 for four and 20 for five. For a single range over 12 kW up to 27 kW, increase the Column C value by 5 percent for each additional kilowatt or major fraction above 12.

front: Find the demand for one 14 kilowatt household electric range, and the 240 volt current.
back: The range exceeds 12 kilowatts by 2, so increase the Column C value of 8 kilowatts by 10 percent: 8 times 1.10 equals 8.8 kilowatts. Current is 8,800 divided by 240, or 36.7 amperes, so a 40 ampere circuit applies.

front: A 12 kilowatt range at 240 volts would draw 50 amperes at full rating. What is its calculated branch circuit load?
back: 8 kilowatts from the Column C demand, which at 240 volts is 33.3 amperes. A 40 ampere breaker with 8 AWG copper is enough. Ranges and dryers use demand tables, not the 125 percent continuous rule.

front: If the range demand is 8,800 volt amperes, what is the neutral load at 70 percent, and in amperes at 240 volts?
back: 0.70 times 8,800 equals 6,160 volt amperes. Divided by 240 volts, that is 25.7 amperes of feeder neutral demand. The neutral carries only the 120 volt portion of the load, such as clock, lights and controls. A branch circuit neutral follows its own 70 percent of circuit rating rule, minimum 10 AWG.

front: What is the household dryer load rule, and what demand factor applies to 1 to 4 dryers?
back: Use 5,000 volt amperes or the nameplate rating, whichever is larger. Demand is 100 percent for 1 to 4 dryers, then 85 percent for 5, 75 for 6, 65 for 7, 60 for 8, 55 for 9, 50 for 10 and 47 for 11 dryers.

front: Find the demand load for 8 household dryers rated 5.5 kVA each.
back: Each dryer is above the 5 kVA minimum, so use 5.5. Connected load is 8 times 5.5, which is 44 kVA. The 8 dryer demand factor is 60 percent, so 44 times 0.60 equals 26.4 kVA. Using 5 kVA each gives 24 kVA, which is wrong.

front: What demand factor applies to 40 dryers at 5.6 kVA each, and what is the demand load?
back: For 24 to 42 dryers the factor is 35 percent less 0.5 percent for each dryer over 23. Forty is 17 over 23, so 35 minus 8.5 equals 26.5 percent. Connected is 224 kVA, and 224 times 0.265 equals 59.4 kVA.

front: What does the 2026 NEC change about the arc flash label in 110.16?
back: It is now an arc flash hazard marking, and the 1,000 ampere threshold is gone: all service and feeder supplied equipment other than in dwelling units needs it. It shows nominal voltage, arc flash boundary, incident energy or PPE level, and assessment date, and cannot be handwritten.

front: What did the 2026 NEC change about GFCI for outdoor dwelling unit outlets in 210.8?
back: The threshold rose from 50 amperes to 60 amperes: GFCI protection is required for outdoor outlets rated 60 amperes or less at dwelling units. A temporary exception covers listed HVAC equipment before September 1, 2026. Confirm these dates in your 2026 NEC.

front: In the 2026 NEC, how did Article 220 change, and what does the readily accessible definition now say?
back: Article 220 became Article 120, so range and dryer demand tables you knew as 220.55 and 220.54 now sit in Article 120. Readily accessible means reachable quickly without tools other than a key, climbing over or under barriers, removing obstacles or using portable ladders.

front: A motor nameplate and the full load current tables both show current. Which one sizes the branch circuit conductors, and which sizes the overload device?
back: Tables size the conductors, short circuit protection and disconnect. The nameplate current sizes the overload device only. A nameplate figure given in a conductor question is bait, because the table value is what the code requires for conductor sizing.

front: What does a service factor of 1.15 on a motor nameplate mean, and what does it change in your calculations?
back: The motor may be run at 115 percent of its rated load without damage. It changes the overload setting: a motor with a marked service factor of 1.15 or more gets an overload device set at no more than 125 percent of nameplate current.

front: What does the code letter on a motor nameplate tell you, and which calculation uses it?
back: The code letter gives the locked rotor kVA per horsepower, the current the motor pulls at the instant of starting. It feeds the locked rotor calculation and generator sizing for motor starting. Letter G covers 5.6 to 6.29 kVA per horsepower.

front: A question mentions no design letter for a motor. Which design do you assume, and what does the design letter affect?
back: Assume design B, the common general purpose motor. The design letter changes which locked rotor table applies and changes the maximum setting for an instantaneous trip breaker. Energy efficient design B gets a higher instantaneous trip maximum in Table 430.52.

front: What is locked rotor current, and is it used to size motor branch circuit conductors?
back: Locked rotor current is the very high current a motor draws at the instant of starting or when the rotor is jammed, often six or more times full load current. It is not used for conductor sizing. It matters for the disconnecting means in 430.110 and generator sizing.

front: In motor circuit rules, what does the phrase 'in sight' mean for a disconnecting means?
back: In sight means visible and not more than 50 feet away, per 110.29 and Article 100. Each motor and its controller need a disconnecting means in sight of the controller. The motor itself also needs one in sight, unless a lockable controller disconnect meets the exception.

front: What is the difference between a motor controller and a motor disconnecting means? Can one device be both?
back: The controller starts and stops the motor in normal operation and needs a horsepower rating at least equal to the motor. The disconnect lets you cut power for service. One device can be both, such as a listed manual motor controller marked suitable as a disconnect. A plain contactor is not a disconnect.

front: What is a motor control center, and what does each unit in the lineup contain?
back: A motor control center, or MCC, is a factory built assembly that gathers many motor starters in one lineup with a common bus. Each unit holds a starter, an overload device, and a disconnect or circuit breaker, so each unit still has its own branch circuit protection.

front: Which article covers emergency systems, what kinds of loads do they serve, and how fast must power return?
back: Article 700 covers emergency systems. They serve loads whose loss threatens life safety, such as exit and egress lighting, fire pumps and fire alarm systems. Power must be restored within 10 seconds. Confirm the exact time limit in your 2026 NEC.

front: What is a legally required standby system, which article covers it, and what is its restoration time?
back: A legally required standby system powers loads that a government rule requires to keep running, such as smoke control or some communication systems. It is covered by Article 701 and must restore power within 60 seconds. Confirm the time limit in your 2026 NEC.

front: What is an optional standby system, and does it have a required transfer time limit?
back: Article 702 covers optional standby systems. They serve loads whose loss may cause inconvenience or financial loss, such as a home, a farm or a data room. There is no required time limit, and transfer may be manual, unlike emergency and legally required systems, which use automatic transfer.

front: When is a generator treated as a separately derived system, and what does it then need?
back: A generator is separately derived when its transfer switch switches the neutral, opening it along with the phases, such as a four pole switch on a three phase four wire system. It then needs its own system bonding jumper, a grounding electrode connection and a grounded conductor connection per 250.30.

front: In the 2026 NEC, what shorter name may replace 'short circuit and ground fault protective device' in Article 430?
back: The 2026 code uses the term OCPD, meaning overcurrent protective device. A question may use OCPD and the older wording interchangeably. The device still protects against faults, not slow overload, and Table 430.52 still sets its maximum rating or setting.

front: What is the minimum ampacity for branch circuit conductors supplying a single continuous duty motor, and what current do you apply it to?
back: Conductors need an ampacity of at least 125 percent of the motor full load current taken from the table, per 430.22. Use the table value for horsepower, voltage and phase, then pick the conductor from Table 310.16 in the correct temperature column.

front: List the Table 430.52 maximum percentages of table full load current for the four common branch circuit protective device types.
back: Nontime delay fuse: 300 percent. Dual element time delay fuse: 175 percent. Inverse time circuit breaker: 250 percent. Instantaneous trip breaker, allowed only in a listed motor controller combination: 800 percent for design B, 1100 percent for energy efficient design B.

front: What overload percentages apply to a continuous duty motor over 1 horsepower under 430.32(A)(1), and when does each apply?
back: Use 125 percent of nameplate current when the motor has a service factor of 1.15 or more, or a marked temperature rise of 40 degrees Celsius or less. All other motors get 115 percent. Check the nameplate for both conditions before choosing.

front: When may an overload device be set higher than the normal 125 or 115 percent, and what are the higher limits?
back: Only when the normal setting will not let the motor start or carry its load. Section 430.32(C) then allows up to 140 percent for service factor 1.15 or more, or temperature rise 40 degrees or less, and up to 130 percent for all others. The question must say the motor trips.

front: What is the minimum ampere rating of a motor disconnecting means, and what extra requirement applies to horsepower rated switches?
back: The disconnecting means must be rated at least 115 percent of the motor full load current from the table. A horsepower rated switch must also carry a horsepower rating at least equal to the motor horsepower at the motor voltage, per 430.109 and 430.110.

front: How do you size feeder conductors that supply several motors under 430.24?
back: Take 125 percent of the full load current of the largest motor, then add the full load currents of all the other motors at 100 percent. Use table currents for every motor. Other loads on the same feeder are added at their own calculated percentage.

front: What percentage of generator nameplate current sets the minimum generator output conductor ampacity, and which section says so?
back: Section 445.13 requires an ampacity of at least 115 percent of the generator nameplate current rating, unless the generator design prevents overloading. Motors use 125 percent, so do not mix the two percentages.

front: A motor is rated 230 volts on a 240 volt system. Which voltage column of the full load current tables do you use?
back: Use the 230 volt column. Match the motor rating, not the system voltage, to the table column. A 460 volt motor on a 480 volt system uses the 460 column, and a 208 volt motor uses the 208 column. There is no 240 volt column.

front: Under what conditions may a manually started motor of 1 horsepower or less be protected by the branch circuit device alone?
back: When the motor is not automatically started and is in sight of the controller, 430.32(D) allows the branch circuit protective device alone to serve as overload protection. Automatically started motors still need their own overload protection, even at a fraction of a horsepower.

front: A 10 horsepower, 230 volt, three phase motor is continuous duty. The 230 volt column gives 28 amperes. What copper conductor size is required in the 75 degree column?
back: 28 times 1.25 equals 35 amperes. In the 75 degree column of Table 310.16, 10 AWG carries 35 amperes, which equals the requirement, so it passes. The conductor is 10 AWG copper. Equal ampacity is enough.

front: A 5 horsepower, 230 volt single phase motor has a table full load current of 28 amperes. What is the maximum standard size inverse time breaker?
back: Use the 250 percent column of Table 430.52: 28 times 2.5 equals 70 amperes. That is already a standard size, so the maximum inverse time breaker is 70 amperes, with no need to round up to the next size.

front: The same 5 horsepower, 230 volt single phase motor has 28 amperes table current. What is the maximum dual element fuse size?
back: Dual element fuses may be 175 percent: 28 times 1.75 equals 49 amperes. That is not a standard size, so go to the next standard size of 240.6(A) for a branch circuit maximum. The maximum dual element fuse is 50 amperes.

front: A motor has a nameplate current of 18.4 amperes, service factor 1.0 and a marked temperature rise of 50 degrees Celsius. What is the maximum normal overload setting?
back: Neither the service factor of 1.15 nor the 40 degree temperature rise condition applies, so use 115 percent. 18.4 times 1.15 equals 21.16 amperes. That is the maximum normal overload setting from the nameplate current.

front: A 10 horsepower, 230 volt, three phase motor has code letter G, which is 5.6 kVA per horsepower at the low end. Find the minimum locked rotor current.
back: Locked rotor kVA is 10 times 5.6, or 56 kVA. Three phase current equals kVA times 1000 divided by 1.732 times voltage. 1.732 times 230 equals 398.36, and 56,000 divided by 398.36 equals about 140.6 amperes.

front: A 460 volt three phase feeder serves 40, 25 and 10 horsepower motors with table currents of 52, 34 and 14 amperes. Find the minimum feeder ampacity.
back: Largest motor is the 40 horsepower: 52 times 1.25 equals 65 amperes. Add the others: 34 plus 14 equals 48. Total is 113 amperes. In the 75 degree column, 2 AWG carries 115 amperes, so the feeder is 2 AWG copper.

front: For the 40, 25 and 10 horsepower, 460 volt feeder, inverse time branch breakers are 150, 90 and 35 amperes. What is the maximum feeder protection?
back: Take the largest branch device, 150 amperes, and add the full load currents of the other motors: 34 plus 14 equals 48. The maximum is 198 amperes. It falls between 175 and 200, and 430.62 is a maximum, so round down to 175 amperes.

front: A 15 horsepower, 230 volt three phase motor has a table current of 42 amperes. What minimum rating does the disconnecting means need?
back: 42 times 1.15 equals 48.3 amperes, so the switch needs at least 48.3 amperes, which means the next standard switch size of 60 amperes. It must also be horsepower rated for at least 15 horsepower at 230 volts.

front: A three phase 208 volt generator is rated 75 kVA. Find its nameplate current and the minimum output conductor size in the 75 degree column.
back: 1.732 times 208 equals 360.26, and 75,000 divided by 360.26 equals 208.2 amperes. Times 1.15 gives 239.4 amperes. 4/0 AWG carries 230, too small, so use 250 kcmil copper at 255 amperes.

front: A single phase 240 volt, 20 kW generator has a power factor of 1.0. What is the minimum conductor size in the 75 degree column?
back: Current is 20,000 divided by 240, or 83.3 amperes. Times 1.15 under 445.13 gives 95.8 amperes. 3 AWG carries 100 amperes in the 75 degree column, which is enough. The conductor is 3 AWG copper.

front: A generator must start a 10 horsepower code letter G motor, using the high end of 62.9 locked rotor kVA, with 20 kVA of other running load. Find the minimum kVA.
back: Add the locked rotor kVA of the motor to the other running load: 20 plus 62.9 equals 82.9 kVA at the moment of starting. Real engineers also allow for voltage dip using manufacturer curves, but the exam keeps it at this level.

front: Three 460 volt motors on one feeder are 50, 30 and 20 horsepower, with table currents of 65, 40 and 27 amperes. What is the feeder ampacity?
back: Only the largest motor gets 125 percent: 65 times 1.25 equals 81.25. Add 40 plus 27, which is 67. The total is 148.25 amperes. Applying 125 percent to every motor would give 165 amperes, which oversizes the feeder.

front: Which device protects a motor from a slow overload, and which protects it from a short circuit or ground fault?
back: The overload relay or heater protects against slow overload, and the branch circuit short circuit and ground fault protective device protects against faults. The exam likes to swap them. A fuse sized at 175 percent does not protect against overload.

front: A question gives a nameplate current of 32.5 amperes for a 25 horsepower, 460 volt motor and asks for the conductor. What current do you use?
back: Use the table value of 34 amperes from Table 430.250, not 32.5. The nameplate current is only for the overload device. Then multiply 34 by 1.25 to get 42.5 amperes before choosing the conductor.

front: A feeder protection calculation under 430.62 gives 198 amperes. Why is 175 amperes the answer and 200 amperes the trap?
back: The 430.62 percentage rule is a maximum, so you round down to the largest standard size that does not exceed it. For a branch circuit the exception lets you go up. For a feeder, an answer of 200 exceeds the permitted maximum.

front: A candidate applies 125 percent to every motor on a multiple motor feeder. What is wrong with that?
back: Only the largest motor, the one with the largest full load current, is taken at 125 percent. All other motors count at 100 percent of table current. Applying 125 percent to every motor oversizes the feeder conductors.

front: A dual voltage motor is marked 20 amperes at 230 volts and 10 amperes at 460 volts. Which current do you use?
back: Use the one that matches the connected voltage. The motor draws half the current at 460 volts that it draws at 230. For the overload setting use the matching nameplate current, and for conductors and protection use the tables at the connected voltage.

front: A motor is fed by a variable frequency drive. How are the conductors to the drive and from the drive to the motor sized?
back: Conductors to the drive input are at least 125 percent of the drive rated input current, per 430.122. Conductors from the drive to the motor are still 125 percent of the motor table current. Check whether the drive provides overload protection.

front: Where in your code book do you find full load current for motors, and which table fits which motor type?
back: Look in the back of Article 430. Table 430.248 is single phase, Table 430.250 is three phase induction motors, and Table 430.247 is direct current. Tab these pages before the exam. Always check which table first, because the same horsepower gives very different current.

front: Does the 2026 110.16 arc flash marking apply to a feeder supplied motor control center in a commercial building?
back: Yes. The 1,000 ampere threshold is removed, so all service and feeder supplied equipment in other than dwelling units needs the marking. It shows nominal voltage, arc flash boundary, incident energy or PPE level, and assessment date, and cannot be handwritten.

front: In the 2026 NEC, what must be at the service disconnect when a standby generator's disconnect is in a different place?
back: Section 230.70(D) requires a plaque or directory at the service disconnect identifying the location of all energy source disconnecting means. The generator disconnect in 445.18 is one of the examples cited, along with 480.7, 705.20 and 706.15.

front: A motor question also includes lighting loads on the same feeder. Which article holds the load calculation rules in the 2026 NEC?
back: Article 120, because Article 220 is now Article 120 in the 2026 NEC. If a question cites 220 numbers from an older book, translate to Article 120. Confirm the section numbers in your printed 2026 NEC.

front: What does the 2026 NEC definition of readily accessible require, and how does it differ from plain accessible?
back: Readily accessible means reachable quickly and without extra actions: no tools other than a key, no climbing over or under barriers, no removing obstacles, no portable ladder. Accessible only means a person can get to it, even if they must move things or climb. A disconnect behind stacked pallets is accessible but not readily accessible.

front: What two conditions must both be met for a device to be within sight of equipment?
back: It must be visible and not more than 50 feet away. Both conditions are required. A disconnect 30 feet away behind a solid wall fails because it cannot be seen. A disconnect 70 feet away across an open yard fails because it is too far, even though it is clearly visible.

front: What is the difference between a contactor and a motor starter?
back: A contactor is an electrically operated switch that carries motor current when its coil is energized. A starter is a contactor with an overload relay attached. A contactor alone gives no overload protection. If an exam question includes an overload relay, the device is a starter.

front: What two ratings must a motor disconnect meet under 430.110, and which current is used for the ampere rating?
back: The horsepower rating must be at least the motor horsepower, and the ampere rating must be at least 115 percent of the motor full load current. Use the table current, Table 430.248 for single phase or Table 430.250 for three phase, not the nameplate current.

front: An ac general use snap switch controls a motor of 2 hp or less. What limit applies to the motor full load current?
back: The motor full load current must not exceed 80 percent of the switch ampere rating, and the motor must be 2 horsepower or less and 300 volts or less. The switch must also be marked with its ratings. Confirm the section number in your 2026 NEC, because small switch type wiring devices moved from Article 404 into Article 406.

front: A 1 hp, 115 volt, single phase motor has a Table 430.248 full load current of 16 amperes. What is the smallest general use snap switch rating?
back: 20 amperes. The motor current may not exceed 80 percent of the switch rating, so divide 16 by 0.80, which equals 20 amperes. A 15 ampere switch fails and a 20 ampere switch passes. This is a one step division using the table current.

front: A 10 hp, 460 volt, three phase motor has a nameplate current of 13.2 A, service factor 1.15, and Table 430.250 current of 14 A. Find the maximum overload setting and maximum inverse time breaker.
back: Overload: 13.2 times 1.25 equals 16.5 amperes, using the nameplate because the service factor is 1.15. Breaker: 14 times 2.50 equals 35 amperes, using the table current, and 35 is a standard size in 240.6(A). Overload uses nameplate, breaker uses table.

front: A 25 hp, 460 volt, three phase motor has a Table 430.250 current of 34 A. Find the inverse time breaker and dual element fuse maximums.
back: Breaker: 34 times 2.50 equals 85 amperes, which is not standard, so go up to the next standard size, 90 amperes. Fuse: 34 times 1.75 equals 59.5 amperes, so the next standard size, 60 amperes, is permitted. The tolerant dual element fuse uses the lower percentage.

front: A 24 volt Class 2 transformer is marked 100 volt amperes. What is its maximum current, and what happens if the load draws 5 amperes?
back: Maximum current is 100 divided by 24, which equals 4.17 amperes. A 5 ampere load exceeds that, so the source is overloaded and will go into protection. Class 2 circuits are power limited by their source, which is why the volt ampere rating sets the current ceiling.

front: What does 110.25 require for a disconnecting means that must be lockable?
back: It must be capable of being locked in the open position, and the provision for locking must remain in place with or without the lock installed. The hasp or lock opening is built in, not an add on. Lockout procedure is a work practice standard outside the NEC, and a lock does not prove the circuit is dead.

front: Which current goes where: nameplate or table current, when sizing a motor circuit?
back: Use the nameplate current only for the overload relay. Use the table current, Table 430.248 or 430.250, for nearly every other step: disconnect, breaker or fuse, and conductor. Using nameplate current where table current belongs is the most common wrong answer on motor sizing questions.

front: A shunt trip breaker is operated by a remote pushbutton at a dwelling. Is the pushbutton the service disconnecting means?
back: No. Section 230.70(F) says a remote control device, such as a pushbutton operating a shunt trip breaker, is not a service disconnecting means. The breaker is the disconnect, and for one and two family dwellings it must be readily accessible, outdoors, and marked EMERGENCY DISCONNECT. The pushbutton is only a convenience.

front: What does a Class I hazardous location contain, and what are two examples?
back: Flammable gases or vapors, including vapors from flammable or combustible liquids. Examples are a paint mixing room, a refinery pump area or a gas station dispenser. Class I is the gas and vapor class; dust is Class II and fibers are Class III.

front: What does a Class II hazardous location contain, and what are two examples?
back: Combustible dust. Examples are a grain elevator, a flour mill or a facility that handles metal powders. If the stem says dust, think Class II. Gas or vapor means Class I, and fibers or flyings mean Class III.

front: What does a Class III hazardous location contain, and does it have Groups?
back: Easily ignitible fibers or flyings, such as in a textile mill or a woodworking shop with lots of shavings. The fibers collect around equipment instead of hanging in the air. Class III has no Groups.

front: What is the difference between Division 1 and Division 2 in a classified location?
back: Division 1 means the hazard is present under normal operation, during frequent repair, or when a breakdown could release it. Division 2 means it is only present when something goes wrong, like a leaking container. Division tells you how likely the hazard is, not how dangerous the material is.

front: Which materials are in Class I Groups A, B, C and D?
back: Group A is acetylene. Group B is hydrogen and similar gases. Group C includes ethylene and similar materials. Group D is the common one: gasoline, propane, natural gas, methane and most common solvents. Equipment must be listed for the Group of the material present.

front: Which materials fall in Class II Groups E, F and G?
back: Group E is metal dust. Group F is carbon-based dust such as coal and carbon black. Group G is grain, flour, starch, plastic and other non-conductive dust. A grain bin with dust in suspension during loading is Class II, Division 1, Group G.

front: How do Zone 0, Zone 1 and Zone 2 describe gas and vapor hazards?
back: Zone 0: an ignitible concentration is present continuously or for long periods. Zone 1: likely under normal operation, or often during repair. Zone 2: not likely in normal operation, and only for a short time if it occurs. Zones 0 and 1 roughly match Division 1; Zone 2 roughly matches Division 2.

front: In the zone system, which gas group is most hazardous: IIA, IIB or IIC?
back: IIC is the most hazardous and covers acetylene and hydrogen. IIB covers ethylene and similar gases. IIA is the lightest and covers propane, gasoline and similar gases. The zone letters run opposite to the Class I Groups A to D, so do not mix the two systems.

front: What is intrinsic safety, and how is an intrinsically safe circuit often identified?
back: Intrinsic safety limits electrical and thermal energy in a circuit so low that it cannot ignite the atmosphere even under fault. Article 504 covers it. These circuits must be kept separate from other circuits and are often identified with the color light blue.

front: What do purge Types X, Y and Z each do to the classification inside an enclosure?
back: Type X reduces Division 1 to unclassified, so it is the strongest. Type Y reduces Division 1 to Division 2. Type Z reduces Division 2 to unclassified, so it is the lightest. Purging uses clean air or inert gas at slight positive pressure.

front: What is explosionproof equipment designed to do?
back: It contains an explosion inside its enclosure and cools the escaping gases enough that they cannot ignite the atmosphere outside. This is the classic Division 1 approach, using heavy cast enclosures and threaded joints.

front: What does a Category 1 space mean in a health care facility, and what are examples?
back: A space where failure of equipment or the electrical system is likely to cause major injury or death to patients, staff or visitors. Examples are operating rooms and intensive care units. The facility's governing body chooses the category with the designer.

front: What does the life safety branch of a hospital essential electrical system supply?
back: Loads needed for safe egress: exit signs, egress lighting, fire alarm and alarm systems, emergency communications and generator set locations. It must be independent of all other wiring so a fault in a lesser circuit never darkens egress lighting.

front: What does the critical branch supply, and which branch serves a nurse call system?
back: The critical branch supplies loads affecting patient care: task illumination, selected receptacles in patient care and critical care areas, and equipment such as the nurse call system. A nurse call system is a patient care function, so it goes on the critical branch.

front: What is an isolated power system in a hospital wet procedure location?
back: An ungrounded system fed through an isolation transformer with a line isolation monitor that alarms when leakage current rises to a set threshold. A ground fault on one conductor does not trip a breaker, so the operating room keeps its power.

front: What is duty cycle for an arc welder?
back: The percentage of a ten-minute period during which the welder can operate at rated output without overheating. A welder at 50 percent duty cycle can weld five minutes out of every ten. A lower duty cycle allows smaller supply conductors than the nameplate current suggests.

front: What is the agricultural equipotential plane and why is it required?
back: Wire mesh or other conductive elements embedded in concrete floors of livestock confinement areas, bonded to the building grounding system with solid copper, usually 8 AWG. It prevents stray voltage, because animals are sensitive to small voltage differences between metal stalls and the floor.

front: Which article covers optional standby systems, and what is the central rule for the transfer equipment?
back: Article 702. The transfer equipment must prevent interconnection of the normal and standby sources, so a generator cannot back-feed the utility lines and endanger a line worker. Transfer may be manual, and a sign at the service equipment must show where the standby source is.

front: Within how many inches of the enclosure must a seal be placed, and what may not sit between them?
back: Within 18 inches of the enclosure. No union, coupling, box or fitting is permitted between the seal and the enclosure it protects, except reducers at the seal. The chapter gives 501.15 as the long-standing location; confirm the number in your 2026 NEC.

front: What are the rules for sealing compound in a Class I seal fitting?
back: The compound must be listed, resist the surrounding atmosphere and liquids, and not melt below 93 degrees Celsius (200 degrees Fahrenheit). Its thickness cannot be less than the fitting trade size and never less than 5/8 inch. No splices or taps are allowed in the seal fitting.

front: How many threads must be engaged in threaded joints for Class I, Division 1 wiring, and why?
back: At least five full threads, made wrench-tight. The threads cool the escaping gas if an explosion occurs inside the raceway. Division 1 methods include threaded rigid metal conduit, threaded intermediate metal conduit, and Type MI and MC-HL cable with proper fittings.

front: At a motor fuel dispenser, how is the area around the dispenser classified under Article 514?
back: The inside of the dispenser enclosure is Class I, Division 1. Around it is Class I, Division 2: within 18 inches horizontally of the enclosure and up to 18 inches above grade, and out to 20 feet horizontally from any edge, up to 18 inches above grade. Confirm numbers in your 2026 book.

front: Where must the emergency shutoff for motor fuel dispensers be located?
back: In a clearly marked, accessible location not less than 20 feet and not more than 100 feet from the dispensers. It shuts off power to all dispensers at once, so a person fleeing a fire can reach it. Confirm the numbers in your 2026 book.

front: What are the transfer times for Article 700 emergency systems and Article 701 legally required standby systems?
